title: AC · every 3 weeks

agents.name: Doxorubicin
agents.explanation: Doxorubicin interferes with enzymes and DNA processes needed for cell division. It can also affect heart muscle, so the team considers previous exposure and cardiac risk.
agents.watch: Report pain or burning at the infusion site immediately. New breathlessness or chest symptoms need prompt review. Red urine for a short time can be a drug-colour effect; pain, clots or persistent bleeding still need advice.
risks: Low counts, infection and mouth ulcers
Severe tissue injury if the infusion leaks

agents.name: Cyclophosphamide
agents.explanation: Cyclophosphamide is activated in the body and damages DNA. This helps stop dividing cancer cells but can also affect blood-cell production and reproductive tissues.
agents.watch: Use the prescribed anti-sickness and hydration plan. Report fever, painful urination or blood in the urine.

purpose: This treatment is part of a plan to reduce the chance of breast cancer returning.
schedule_summary: Doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide on Day 1 every 21 days for four cycles. Any subsequent taxane follows a separately agreed regimen.

phases_title: The phases and how they connect
phases_note: Each phase has its own medicines, checks and supportive prescription. A change of phase does not restart the cardiac monitoring clock.
timeline_note: These broad symptom bands are educational possibilities, not measured risk curves. Infusion days are the planned schedule; delays require a new clinical plan.
safety_note: Fever, shivers, sudden illness, severe breathing changes or chest pain need prompt assessment on any day.
teachback: Which phase are you in, what changes next, and who is arranging and reviewing your next blood test, echo or scan?
consent_support: Discuss treatment aim, alternatives, uncertainty, fertility, contraception, access, phase changes, serious and lasting risks, supportive medicines and the urgent contact plan.
urgent_extra: Report new breathing symptoms, severe diarrhoea, inability to drink, painful swollen limbs, unusual bleeding, or worsening numbness. Tell staff immediately about infusion-site pain or an allergic reaction.

support.title: Tests and appointments
support.text: The team should name the booking owner, due window and person reviewing each required test. Tell them if an expected appointment has not arrived.

support.title: After chemotherapy
support.text: Discuss recovery, fertility, rehabilitation and the next treatment or surveillance step.

questions.a: Doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide on Day 1 every 21 days for four cycles. Any subsequent taxane follows a separately agreed regimen.

Baseline cardiac assessment before AC. Repeat imaging according to symptoms, anthracycline exposure and cardiac risk; no universal 12-week echo schedule is assigned to AC alone. ESC guidance supplements the source: baseline echo before anthracyclines; high / very-high cardiac risk may need echo every two cycles and within 3 months after treatment. Test timing follows the treatment, clinical findings and local pathway.

questions.q: Where do surgery and radiotherapy fit?
questions.a: In adjuvant care, radiotherapy usually follows chemotherapy when indicated; endocrine therapy follows its own receptor-specific plan.

questions.q: Do I need routine CT scans or tumour markers?
questions.a: Early breast follow-up uses planned breast imaging. Routine CT / PET, blood tumour markers or other distant-recurrence screening are not recommended without symptoms or a clinical indication. After local treatment: annual mammography of remaining breast tissue; additional imaging when indicated.

questions.q: Does a port mean a pump at home?
questions.a: No. This regimen has no routine take-home infusion pump. A port is an access device; the team removes the needle after the visit when appropriate and arranges device removal separately.

steps.title: Before the first visit
steps.text: Blood tests, relevant cardiac assessment, medicines review, fertility discussion and the consent conversation come first.

steps.title: Plan venous access
steps.text: A cannula, PICC or implanted port may be used. If a port is chosen, a trained team inserts it in a separate procedure with local anaesthetic and sometimes sedation; the team explains fasting, blood-thinner and wound instructions.

steps.title: Infusion day
steps.text: Staff check the line, give prescribed premedicines and treatment, and observe for reactions. Tell them immediately about burning, pain, rash or breathlessness.

steps.title: Home and next review
steps.text: This regimen does not routinely need a take-home infusion pump. Staff disconnect the infusion; a port is de-accessed when appropriate. Keep line-care and next-visit instructions.

details.title: Port insertion and removal
details.text: The line team explains placement, dressing care and when normal activities can resume. A port is accessed with a special needle during treatment. Removal of the implanted device is a separate planned procedure when no longer needed; do not remove or adjust it yourself.

details.title: PICC care and urgent line symptoms
details.text: A PICC usually needs regular dressing and flushing appointments even between treatments. Fever, redness, swelling, pain, leakage or damage requires prompt advice. Your hospital supplies the exact care instructions.

details.title: Visit time and transport
details.text: First visits can take longer because of loading doses, premedicines and observation. Ask the unit about expected time, transport and any escort needed after sedation or line insertion.

details.title: Phase-specific visit pattern
details.text: Infusion and observation times differ by drug and first versus later doses; the unit confirms the full visit duration, including blood review and preparation.
